answer.summary: Lochhead’s advice is to define a distinctive problem before promoting a solution, use fresh but understandable language to frame it, and avoid inviting customers to compare you as just another option. Make the category valuable by showing how it addresses a meaningful need in a way that can feel irreplaceable.

sections.heading: Start with the problem and frame it distinctively
sections.content: Spend more time on the problem than the solution. Define the problem in a way that leads to a different solution set: his example is Gojo asking how to wash hands without water, which led to the hand-sanitizer category and Purell. He says a company that gets people to agree on its definition of the problem—and thereby its definition of the solution—can design the space.

sections.heading: Create language that is new but still understandable
sections.content: Use “languaging”—the strategic use of language to change thinking. Don’t describe a new offering only with old language, but don’t introduce so much unfamiliar language that people can’t tell what you mean. Meet the category where it is and bring people forward with new language.

sections.heading: Differentiate instead of inviting a feature comparison
sections.content: Lochhead describes category design as radical differentiation. Rather than lining up competitors and claiming more features, aim to be irreplaceable and create enough value in customers’ minds that they wonder what they would switch to. One way to reframe demand is to redirect people from what they think they want toward what they need: he illustrates this with spinning classes and Peloton presenting alternatives to outdoor biking and driving to the gym, respectively.

sections.content: He calls the strategic use of language to change thinking “languaging.” Don’t describe a new offering only with old language, but don’t use so much unfamiliar language that people can’t understand it either: meet the category where it is and bring people forward with new language. [S1]

sections.heading: Differentiate from the status quo, not just competitors
sections.content: Avoid framing the offer as a list of features that beats competing products. Lochhead says category designers compete against the status quo and seek to be valuable and distinctive enough to stand alone, rather than inviting direct comparison. His “damming the demand” example: indoor biking classes reframed cycling around getting exercise without the risk of riding on roads; Peloton then asked why people should drive to a gym when they could work out at home. [S5, S6, S4]

sections.heading: Synthesis: make the category’s point of view customer-centered and easy to repeat
sections.content: Put together, the practical approach is to articulate a distinct point of view about customers’ problems and a different solution, then make that point of view quick to express. Lochhead says a category point of view should be about customers, not the company, and that concise articulation can help word of mouth spread. [S8]

answer.summary: Lochhead’s advice is to define a valuable customer problem, reframe it in distinctive language, and compete with the status quo rather than invite product comparisons.

sections.heading: Start with a problem customers value
sections.content: Spend more time on the problem than the solution. Focus on a meaningful customer problem and use it to define a new solution space: Gojo asked how to wash hands without water, leading to hand sanitizer. Lochhead says a solution must fit a problem of value to people.

sections.heading: Make the category feel different through language and framing
sections.content: Use “languaging”—the strategic use of language to change thinking. Don’t describe a new offering only with old language, but don’t use so much unfamiliar language that people cannot understand it; meet people where the category is and bring them forward. Reframe the problem around what customers need: spinning redirected people concerned about cycling risks toward indoor classes, while Peloton asked why they should drive to a gym to work out.

sections.heading: Avoid comparison; make the value stand on its own
sections.content: Rather than invite feature-by-feature comparison with competitors, compete against the status quo and aim to be irreplaceable in customers’ minds. A clear category point of view should be quickly expressible, about customers rather than the company, and give people language they can repeat—supporting word of mouth.
